routes.description: Establish that empirical inquiry has genuine domain limits, that rational guidance may include probabilistic and faith-informed inference about existential and moral questions, and that conservative institutions and market mechanisms can translate such guidance into social policy.
routes.successCriteria: The route is completed by connecting the limits of empirical access to a warranted role for nonempirical inference, then showing how objective human features, inherited institutions, voluntary exchange, and incentive-sensitive policy can guide contested questions without requiring empirical certainty.

motionBridge.description: Show that faith-informed inference and conservative consequences can legitimately guide belief and policy where empirical methods underdetermine existential, moral, or institutional questions.

centralBridges.description: Establish that unresolved questions about origins, purpose, morality, and postmortem existence are not exhausted by present empirical inquiry.
Explain when probabilistic reasoning, practical uncertainty, or high-stakes consequences warrant attention to possibilities lacking direct verification.
Connect biological or moral features of human beings to social norms and institutions that are claimed to track those features.
Show how voluntary exchange, dispersed information, competition, and cost awareness can guide welfare policy and justify unequal outcomes.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Identify incentive structures or institutional interests that may complicate reliance on expert consensus or government-administered systems.
Explain why longstanding sex-based or conscience-sensitive arrangements may serve protective purposes that proposed reforms must address.

routes.description: Establish that belief should remain proportionate to publicly accessible evidence, that unsupported supernatural claims retain their burden of proof, and that political and social arrangements should be judged by secular-humanist consequences for autonomy, health, and shared welfare.
routes.successCriteria: The route is completed by distinguishing uncertainty from affirmative unsupported belief, defending empirical correction and relevant expertise, and applying evidence about harm and well-being to religion in public institutions, gender policy, labor, and health care.

motionBridge.description: Show that empirical warrant and secular-humanist consequences provide the appropriate standards for beliefs and policies affecting other people.

centralBridges.description: Require confidence and inference to remain proportionate to available evidence while assigning affirmative supernatural claims their burden of proof.
Defend scientific evidence, relevant expertise, and revisability as the governing means of resolving factual disputes about the natural and social world.
Connect personal autonomy and religious neutrality to the treatment of identity, legislation, and essential public-facing institutions.
Assess markets, wages, health care, and public policy by their consequences for preventable harm, reciprocal dependence, and access to basic goods.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Show why high stakes or imaginable possibilities do not select one religious conclusion when incompatible alternatives remain evidentially unresolved.
Develop measurable, harm-sensitive alternatives where inherited classifications or consumer-market analogies fail to capture relevant human needs.

sections.title: Evidence, uncertainty, and faith-informed inference
sections.rationale: This issue supplies the governing standards for the entire motion: the burden of supernatural claims, the limits of empirical access, proportional confidence, probabilistic inference, and whether practical stakes can warrant belief or action under uncertainty.

sections.title: Scientific authority, correction, and institutional incentives
sections.rationale: This section tests how each route handles contested natural-world claims by examining empirical inference, scientific revisability, expert reliance, funding incentives, and the separation of observed mechanisms from causal or policy conclusions.

sections.title: Gender, human nature, autonomy, and public institutions
sections.rationale: The gender and religious-neutrality disputes apply the competing standards to biological facts, socially constructed identity, welfare evidence, protective institutions, personal conscience, and the obligations of government and community-serving organizations.

sections.title: Markets, inequality, labor, and human welfare
sections.rationale: This issue contrasts voluntary exchange and entrepreneurial value with living-wage and distributional concerns, clarifying whether market consent or broader effects on workers and society should govern political-economic judgments.

sections.title: Health-care access, incentives, and reciprocal social dependence
sections.rationale: Health care provides a concrete policy test of consumer choice, third-party payment, public mandates, professional expertise, preventable suffering, and the extent to which shared welfare creates collective obligations.
